newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - NatWest Markets' Owen becomes casualty.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - NatWest Markets' Owen becomes casualty.

text.p: NatWest Markets chief executive Martin Owen, who resigned on Monday, faced intense pressure as profits fell amid speculation that his National Westminster Bank Plc masters were about to severely clip the wings of its investment bank.

Earlier this year, Owen had to admit that his operation had suffered a 90 million pound ($147 million) loss on derivatives trading and the report into that debacle, due soon, was seen as the trigger for NatWest to edge away from its commitment to "global" investment banking.

But Monday's announcement, after intense media speculation over Owen's future, has pre-empted publication of the independent report into the options trading loss and looked to be an attempt to control shareholder disapproval of NatWest's strategy.

NatWest's commitment to investment banking was recently questioned again when it emerged that NatWest had initiated discussion of a merger with retail bank Abbey National, much to the delight of analysts who saw NatWest Markets' returns as far too low for the amount of capital employed.
The merger talk apparently came to nothing but the market was again confused about where NatWest is going and Monday's statement seemed an attempt to clarify the position.

Owen, who had run the investment banking unit of British banking giant NatWest since 1992, is a friendly, talkative man with a soft Welsh accent who trained as an accountant and takes an active role in the Salvation Army.

Doubts have persisted about NatWest's investment banking strategy which saw aggressive expansion over the last 18 months through several acquisitions which some analysts have criticised as too expensive.

The big spending included major expansion in the United States with the purchase of Greenwich Capital, a bond trading house, for $590 million and mergers and acquisitions specialist Gleacher for $135 million.

But by all accounts, Owen, 49, made a good job of bringing the disparate parts of NatWest Markets together, although, like its investment banking peers, this meant a big rise in costs with more to come.
Some market observers say Owen did have difficulty with the mergers and acquisitions side of the business.
His background would support this view as Owen came to the top via NatWest's treasury and capital markets operations.
After working for American company Dow Corning Corp in Wales, Owen joined Welsh independent TV company HTV before starting his own accountancy and insurance business which he sold in 1979.

Three years of full-time work for the Salvation Army followed although Owen did manage to squeeze in an external doctorate in, ironically enough, risk management from the University of Southern California.
Thus qualified for the financial markets, Owen joined NatWest in 1983 only pausing for a short stint as a financial supervisor in the Isle of Man.
Analysts did not doubt Owen's ability to make the business bigger but they did question the wisdom of trying to emulate the big Wall Street investment banks.

Even under 1996's relatively favourable market conditions, NatWest Markets profits rose by 158 million pounds to 462 million. But when a big 96 million drop in provisions is taken into account, the 62 million pounds left of the rise is more than wiped out by the options loss.
Owen appeared genuinely shocked that the options problem could have begun as long ago as the end of 1994.
"That is clearly unacceptable against the background of incidents at other firms as well," he said at the time. "Fortunately it does seem to be isolated to this area."

Some would say that fortune should not really come into the equation but at least these losses -- 77 million pounds after provisions and bonus cuts are taken into account -- are dwarfed by those posted by Deutsche Morgan Grenfell or Barings.

Owen, who gave up 200,000 pounds of a 500,000 pound bonus because of the options affair, was staunchly supported by NatWest chief executive Derek Wanless but there were persistent rumours that Wanless had become less sympathetic.

There is also speculation that the report into the options loss, which has taken far longer than expected to produce, has been delayed because the affair has been found to involve more people than was originally thought to be the case.
"It is a set-back for Martin in one area. We'll learn a lot from it, get those lessons put into practice and that will make us much stronger," Wanless said in March.
But in the end, Owen and Wanless seem to have come to the conclusion that the business had outgrown the man who put it together.
($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
